pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–7; at the poles daylight and darkness are extreme — in summer the Sun never fully sets (midnight sun) and in winter it never rises (polar night lasting months), unlike home where every day has both light and dark.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS1 Y1 'Seasonal changes' (observe changes across seasons; day length); links to Y5 Earth-Sun-Moon later.
• Standards—US: NGSS 1-ESS1-2 (observe/describe seasonal patterns of the amount of daylight); K-PS3-1 (effect of sunlight).
• Operational details: at this age teach the PHENOMENON, not the axial-tilt cause (that is the 7–9 topic). The vivid contrast: at the poles the Sun can stay up all 'night' in summer and never come up for weeks in winter. Relate to the child's own day, which always has a sunrise and a sunset. Use imagery of playing outside at midnight in bright sunshine, and of a long dark winter lit by stars and the aurora.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) say that at the poles it can be light in the middle of the night in summer; Tier B (6) describe that in polar winter the Sun does not come up for a long time; Tier C (7) contrast the poles with home, where every day has both daytime and night-time.
bestPractices: Contrast explicitly with the child's normal day (always a morning and a night) so the polar extreme stands out
Use two strong images — a bright midnight-sun scene and a dark, starlit/aurora polar-night scene — rather than abstract explanation
Keep to 'what happens', deferring the tilt-of-the-Earth 'why' to the older topic to avoid overload
Tie to feelings/routines: 'How would you sleep if it were sunny at bedtime? Play if it were dark all day?'
Avoid implying the Sun switches off in winter — it is still there but stays below the horizon
keyRepresentations: Side-by-side summer (midnight sun) and winter (polar night) scene pair
A day-clock showing the Sun circling the sky without dipping below the horizon in polar summer
Home-vs-pole comparison strip: normal sunrise/sunset day next to all-day-light and all-day-dark
Aurora-lit winter scene to show the long polar night is not pitch empty
commonMisconceptions: The Sun is switched off in polar winter — it is still there but stays below the horizon for weeks
It is like this everywhere in winter — only near the poles do you get months with no sunrise or no sunset
Midnight sun means it is hot — the Sun stays low, so summers are still cold
Day and night vanish completely — they stretch to extremes but the yearly cycle continues
This is the same as a normal long summer day at home — the poles have the Sun up for the WHOLE 24 hours, not just longer

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: at the poles daylight and darkness reach extremes — in polar summer the Sun stays up even at midnight (midnight sun) and in polar winter it does not rise for weeks or months (polar night), unlike home where every day has both a sunrise and a sunset. Teach the phenomenon ('what happens'), not the axial-tilt cause (a later 7–9 topic). The central aim is for children to grasp that a single polar 'day' or 'night' can last around the full 24-hour clock — not merely a longer day than at home — and that the Sun is never switched off; in winter it simply stays hidden below the horizon.

activities.title: Spin the day at the North Pole
feedback: If the child is surprised the Sun is still up at midnight, confirm: yes — in polar summer the Sun stays above the horizon even in the middle of the night. That is the midnight sun.

If the child thinks the winter scene means the Sun is gone, respond: the Sun is still shining — it is just sitting below the edge of the ground (the horizon), so its direct light does not reach that spot. That is the polar night.
Reinforce the pairing: SUMMER = light all the time (midnight sun); WINTER = dark for a long time (polar night).
activities.rationale: Operating a full day lets the child make the Sun circle and 'feel' the extreme of a Sun that never sets or never rises, which is the striking idea at the heart of the topic. A draggable clock/Sun that keeps the Sun in view at midnight is intended to make the 'never sets' idea concrete. This is one way to present it; a fixed picture can also show the two states but cannot be swept through a whole turn.
sourceClaims: Above the polar circles the Sun remains above the horizon for 24 hours around midsummer (midnight sun) and below it for 24 hours around midwinter (polar night)
learnerActions: Move a clock hand (or a Sun marker) all the way around a full 24-hour day at the North Pole in summer, watching the Sun stay up and circle the sky without ever dipping below the horizon — at 'midnight' it is still shining and a child is playing outside

Flip a summer/winter switch and sweep the same full day again in winter: now the Sun stays hidden below the horizon the whole time, the scene stays dark, and stars and sometimes the aurora can light the sky
Say out loud, after each full turn, what the Sun did — 'it never set' in summer, 'it never came up' in winter
activities.intendedInsight: At the poles a single 'day' or 'night' can last all the way around the clock: in summer the Sun never sets and in winter it never rises — nothing like home, where morning and night always take turns.

activities.title: Home vs. pole comparison strip
feedback: If the child insists the Sun must rise and set every day even at the poles, gently contrast: at home yes, but at and close to the poles there are real stretches of weeks or even months with no sunrise (winter) or no sunset (summer).
Praise accurate contrasts that keep home's daily cycle separate from the polar extreme.
activities.rationale: Explicitly contrasting with the child's own familiar day makes the polar extreme stand out and addresses the misconception that everywhere has the same day and night. This directly supports the Tier C goal of comparing poles with home.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils observe changes across the four seasons and observe/describe how day length varies
Students observe, describe, and predict seasonal patterns of the amount of daylight
learnerActions: Look at or build a side-by-side comparison: your own normal day (a morning sunrise and an evening sunset) next to the pole's all-day-light summer and all-day-dark winter
Point to or state what is the same and what is different: at home, every day has both daytime and night-time; at the poles, light or dark can last for weeks
Finish the sentence 'At home the Sun ___ every day, but at the North Pole in summer the Sun ___.'
activities.intendedInsight: The poles are genuinely different from home: home always takes turns between day and night, while the poles can have months with no sunrise or no sunset.

activities.title: Is the Sun broken? — talk and check
feedback: Correct response: the Sun is not gone or broken — it keeps shining and simply stays below the horizon (hidden below the edge of the ground) during the polar night.
If the child says the Sun turns off or disappears, re-teach: the Sun always shines; in polar night it just sits below the horizon, like being 'down' overnight, but for months.

Note two gentle corrections to keep in mind: the midnight sun does not mean it is hot — the Sun stays low, so polar summers are still cold; and the polar night is not pitch empty — it can be lit by stars and the aurora.
activities.rationale: A direct question about whether the Sun is 'gone or broken' targets the documented 'Sun switches off' misconception and lets the child articulate that darkness comes from the Sun being below the horizon, not from the Sun stopping. Tying it to feelings and routines keeps it age-appropriate.
sourceClaims: Above the polar circles the Sun remains above the horizon for 24 hours around midsummer (midnight sun) and below it for 24 hours around midwinter (polar night)
learnerActions: Answer: 'A friend says in polar winter the Sun switches off, so there is no more Sun. Is the Sun really gone or broken? What is actually happening to make it so dark?'
Explain in your own words where the Sun is during the dark polar winter
Imagine and talk about how it would feel: 'How would you sleep if it were sunny at bedtime? How would you play if it were dark all day?'
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun is never switched off in polar winter — it is still shining but stays below the horizon, so its direct light does not reach that place for weeks. The yearly light-and-dark cycle stretches to extremes but continues.

constraints: Teach the phenomenon ('what happens'), not the axial-tilt cause — the Earth-Sun geometry 'why' belongs to the later 7–9 topic and would overload 5–7 learners.
Do not imply the Sun switches off, goes out, or disappears in winter: it is still shining but stays below the horizon.
Clarify that the midnight sun does not mean warmth — the Sun stays low, so polar summers remain cold.
Avoid suggesting a polar winter is totally empty of light — stars and the aurora can light the long night.
Emphasise the whole-24-hour extreme: a polar summer 'day' or winter 'night' lasts around the full clock, not merely a longer day than at home.

A sorting/matching check (light-or-dark, summer-or-winter) can confirm the pairing but does not by itself build the sense of wonder at a Sun that never sets; use it as a check rather than the main teaching.
A static summer/winter scene pair shows the two states clearly but cannot be swept through a continuous 24-hour turn; treat it as a supporting scaffold if a manipulable day is unavailable.
A 3D Earth-Sun model is not needed at this age and would add the cause-level geometry that belongs with the later 7–9 topic; the felt phenomenon can be taught without it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and all activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
All three cited sources carry verified:false in the source row; treat curriculum-standard and polar-phenomenon claims as unverified here.

The original 'a static picture cannot' / 'better shown by manipulating than described in words' / '3D adds nothing' phrasings were softened to scoped proposals with stated affordances, as catalog fit ratings do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

The NGSS 'seasonal patterns of the amount of daylight' claim was removed from activity 1's sourceClaims because it supports the broad day-length topic rather than that activity's specific mechanism/phenomenon principle.

Activity 2's two curriculum claims (KS1 day-length; NGSS daylight patterns) support the broad day-length topic rather than the specific polar-extreme contrast principle; they are retained only as curriculum anchors, while the polar-extreme itself is directly supported only by the polar-circles claim cited in activities 1 and 3.

At the exact North Pole the Sun circles at a roughly constant, seasonally low altitude rather than visibly rising and falling; the final wording 'stay up and circle the sky without ever dipping below the horizon' is an age-appropriate simplification.

Self-audit of science content: midnight sun/polar night description, 'Sun stays below the horizon', and the 'not hot despite midnight sun' points are internally consistent and preserved; no arithmetic or force/motion content present. No activity asks a child to look toward the Sun or through a cover; the simulated day avoids any unsafe sun-observation.

probeDeeper: In the dark polar winter, is the Sun broken, or is it somewhere you just can't see it?
How is a polar winter different from a normal night at your home?
In polar SUMMER, what surprising thing does the Sun do at midnight?
If the Sun is still shining the whole time, why is it dark at the pole in winter?
assess.correctAnswer: The Sun is NOT gone, broken or switched off — it's still shining as always. In polar winter the Sun simply stays BELOW the horizon (hidden below the edge of the ground) for weeks or months, so its light doesn't reach that spot — that's the polar night. In polar summer the opposite happens: the Sun stays ABOVE the horizon even at midnight (the midnight sun). It's very different from home, where every day has some daylight and some darkness.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The Sun switches off / goes out / disappears in winter' — treats darkness as the Sun stopping.
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Sun always shines; in polar night it just sits below the horizon so its light doesn't reach you — like it being 'down' overnight, but for months.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Sun switches off for the winter, so there's no Sun at all until spring.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says there is no Sun, or the Sun turns off / breaks during polar night.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Everywhere on Earth has the same day and night as home' — can't accept months of daylight/darkness.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast home's daily sunrise/sunset with the poles' months-long day and night; it's a real, extreme difference.
errorPatterns.distractor: Even at the North Pole the Sun rises and sets every single day, just like at home.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists there must be a normal sunrise/sunset each day even at the poles.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mixes up which season is light and which is dark — a pairing slip.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pair it: SUMMER = midnight sun (light), WINTER = polar night (dark). Anchor with a simple summer/winter card.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the Sun stays up all winter / stays down all summer.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the Sun switches off/disappears, or that the poles have ordinary daily day-night.
responseLevels.full: Explains the Sun keeps shining but stays below the horizon in winter (polar night) and above it in summer (midnight sun), and contrasts this with normal daily day-night at home.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the poles have long light and long dark spells but still hints the Sun 'goes away', or muddles which season is which.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: At the North Pole in summer, the Sun stays up in the sky even at midnight; and in winter it's dark for weeks and the Sun doesn't come up at all. A friend says 'in polar winter the Sun switches off, or goes out, so there's no more Sun.' Is the Sun really gone or broken in the polar winter? What is actually happening to make it so dark?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the 'Sun switches off' idea says the Sun is gone or not working; a child with the concept keeps the Sun shining and explains the darkness as the Sun staying below the horizon. Asking 'is the Sun gone or broken' directly targets the documented misconception.
